records.real_world_identity_notes: Dallara F301, the older Dallara Formula 3 chassis used as the F3 Light car in Brazilian F3. Individual F301 cars could carry different engine or series configurations; the identity match here is the Reiza Automobilista F301 subtype, not a claim that every F301 carried identical ancillary hardware.
records.confidence_basis: The Reiza Studios discussion identifies Automobilista F301 as the older Dallara chassis racing in Brazilian F3 and calls its class F3 Light. The independent Brazilian F3 technical article names Dallara F301 as F3 Light. The exact F301 cockpit listing inspected for this pass shows a TIPO F301/TELAIO No 035 plaque. Together these establish the Dallara F301 identity used by the submitted AMS1 subtype; they do not identify a particular real chassis number represented by the simulator.

records.specification_basis: The official Mk8/9 manual specifies non-synchronising face dogs. Under the project derivation rules, a dogbox does not require clutch use for ordinary upshifts or downshifts. The manufacturer manual establishes non-synchronising face dogs; the project derivation rule requires the driver to match revs for clean dog engagement, represented as a required manual blip on downshift. This model treats throttle lift as an upshift technique field; no separate downshift-lift control is applicable. The gearbox evidence is cited for the scoped shift mechanism, while no negative real-car claim is made about a driver’s throttle movement. The Reiza discussion identifies the F301 as five-speed; the exact F301 listing describes a five-speed transaxle; and the Hewland manual documents the Mk8/9 four- or five-forward-gear family. The F3 Light F301 is listed with a Hewland Mk9, and the manufacturer manual specifies non-synchronising face dogs. The project vocabulary normalizes that construction as dogbox. The F3 Light technical row explicitly says Hewland Mk9 in H, and the manufacturer manual specifies mechanically operated H-pattern selection. The established H-pattern gate requires a clutch for a standing start under the project derivation rules, independently of the dogbox’s clutchless shift capability. Automatic blip is modeled as a downshift function; it is not applicable to an upshift. This does not claim that the real car had or lacked an electronic throttle system. Non-synchronising face dogs establish the dogbox construction; ordinary upshifts therefore do not require clutch use under the project derivation rules. Manual blip is modeled as a downshift rev-matching technique and is not applicable to an upshift. The reviewed sources did not establish the remaining technique and wheel fields, which stay unknown in the real-car baseline: /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/integrated_display, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/open_top, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shape, /authentic_controls/steering/wheel_rim/shift_lights, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_blip, /authentic_controls/transmission/downshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/shift_pattern, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/automatic_cut, /authentic_controls/transmission/upshift/throttle_lift.
